system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-06-11 21:16:00 to 2170-06-14 10:38:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for persistent nausea and poor oral intake following gastric bypass surgery, leading to malnutrition and dependence on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). She underwent a laparoscopic gastrostomy tube placement to establish enteral feeding access. Postoperatively, she tolerated tube feeds well, reached goal nocturnal feeding rates, and was weaned off TPN. Her central line was removed, and she began tolerating a stage V diet. She was discharged home with home nursing support for tube feeds, instructions for G-tube care, and a follow-up plan with her surgeon.

Discharge note 1 (2170-06-14 00:00:00): Name:  ___                  Unit No:   ___
 
Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___
 
Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F
 
Service: SURGERY
 
Allergies: 
No Known Allergies / Adverse Drug Reactions
 
Attending: ___.
 
Chief Complaint:
Dry heaves
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
___: EGD

 
History of Present Illness:
___ with very complicated recent medical history.  She is s/p 
gastric bypass in ___, which was complicated by anastomotic 
ulcers.  Her ulcers and pain were so severe as to require 
placement of a ___ catheter for high-dose PPI and TPN, as 
well as a G-tube for nutrition.  Her ___ catheter was 
removed earlier this year, and her G-tube was removed ___ at 
her request.  Since the removal of her G-tube, she has been 
having progressively more abdominal pain, dry heaving, and 
inability to take adequate nutrition.  She was initially having 
dry heaves a few times a week, but is now having them many times 
per day.  She has not had any regurgitation, and has been having 
normal bowel movements, without diarrhea, blood, or melena.  She 
was seen in clinic on ___, at which time she was started on 
Carafate and given a small prescription for dilaudid.  She was 
also scheduled for upper endoscopy to evaluate the anastomosis 
for ___.  She called the office today complaining of continued 
pain and concern that she was not getting adequate nutrition.

 
Past Medical History:
PMH: GERD, PCOS, G-J anastomitic ulcer, h/o C. diff colitis ___

PSH: R carpal tunnel surgery ___, R shoulder surgery ___, 
tubal ligation ___, lap RNY gastric bypass ___, R IJ Hickman 
catheter ___ (removed), appendectomy, lap G-tube placement ___ 
(removed)

 
Social History:
___
Family History:
Her family history remarkable for obesity and CAD
 
Physical Exam:
Physical Exam on Discharge: 

VSS, afebrile 
Gen: AAOx3, NAD, pleasant, comfortable
HEENT: Neck supple, mucous membranes moist
CV: RRR, no murmurs/rubs/gallops
Resp: CTAB
Abd: soft, non-tender, non-distended, well healed surgical 
incisions, + BS
Ext: warm, well-perfused, distal pulses palpable

 
Pertinent Results:

MCV-92 MCH-30.9 MCHC-33.7 RDW-13.5 Plt ___ ___ 06:25AM 
BLOOD Glucose-70 UreaN-6 Creat-0.7 Na-142 K-4.1 Cl-108 HCO3-28 
AnGap-10 ___ 06:25AM BLOOD Calcium-8.7 Phos-3.8 Mg-2.2

___ 06:15PM BLOOD WBC-4.1 RBC-4.18* Hgb-12.9 Hct-38.0 
MCV-91# MCH-30.9 MCHC-34.0 RDW-13.4 Plt ___ Neuts-49.2* 
___ Monos-8.3 Eos-4.4* Baso-0.8 Glucose-86 UreaN-7 
Creat-0.8 Na-141 K-3.6 Cl-103 HCO3-29 AnGap-13 

___: EGD:
-Evidence of previous roux-en-y gastric by pass was noted. 
-A small erosion was seen in the cardia of the gastric remnant. 
-The blind limb appeared unremarkable. 
-The alimentary limb and the jejuno-jejunal anastomosis appeared 
unremarkable
 
Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ presented to the Emergency Department on ___ due to complaints of worsening dry heaves and concern 
regarding her ability to consume adequate nutrition.  
Intravenous fluids including a banana bag were administered and 
the patient was transferred to the general surgical ward once 
deemed stable. 

On hospital day 2, the patient's vital signs remained stable and 
she was able to tolerate a stage 4 bariatric diet without 
incident.  Additionally, she was voiding adequately.  She was 
also given intravenous protonix BID.  On hospital day 3, an 
upper endoscopy was performed, which was essentially normal 
except for a small erosion noted in the gastric pouch. 

At the time of discharge on hospital day 4, the patient was 
doing well, afebrile with stable vital signs.  The patient was 
tolerating a stage 5 diet, ambulating, voiding without 
assistance, and pain was well controlled.  She will continue 
oral pantoprazole and sucralfate.  The patient also received 
pain medication for the next week. The patient received 
discharge teaching and follow-up instructions with understanding 
verbalized and agreement with the discharge plan.  
 
Medications on Admission:
Sucralfate 1 gram QID
Citalopram 40 mg daily
Metoclopramide 10 mg BID
Temazepam 15 mg q HS
Aripiprazole 20 mg daily
Pantoprazole 40 mg daily
 
Discharge Medications:
1. sucralfate 1 gram Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO QID (4 times 
a day).  
2. citalopram 20 mg Tablet Sig: Two (2) Tablet PO DAILY (Daily). 
 
3. lorazepam 1 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO BID (2 times a 
day) as needed for anxiety.  
4. metoclopramide 10 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO BID (2 
times a day) as needed for nausea.  
5. temazepam 15 mg Capsule Sig: Two (2) Capsule PO HS (at 
bedtime).  
6. aripiprazole 10 mg Tablet Sig: Two (2) Tablet PO DAILY 
(Daily).  
7. pantoprazole 40 mg Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) Sig: One 
(1) Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) PO twice a day.  

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
Gastric erosion

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital with complaints of dry 
heaving.  An upper endoscopy was performed --------.  You are 
now preparing for discharge to home with the following 
instructions:

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:
*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.
*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.
*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.
*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.
*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.
*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.
*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.
*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.
*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.
Please resume all regular home medications , unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.
Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids. Avoid lifting 
weights greater than ___ lbs until you follow-up with your 
surgeon.
Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.
Incision Care:
*Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner if you have 
increased pain, swelling, redness, or drainage from the incision 
site.
*Avoid swimming and baths until your follow-up appointment.
*You may shower, and wash surgical incisions with a mild soap 
and warm water. Gently pat the area dry.
*If you have staples, they will be removed at your follow-up 
appointment.
*If you have steri-strips, they will fall off on their own. 
Please remove any remaining strips ___ days after surgery.

 
Followup Instructions:
___

diagnoses.long_title: Other complications of other bariatric procedure
Other specified procedures as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team members. You're here because of worsening dry heaves and trouble keeping food down. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. It started a few weeks ago—just a few dry heaves a week. But now it’s several times a day. I can’t eat much without feeling like I’m going to heave again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any vomiting with actual content, or just dry heaves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just dry heaves. No vomiting. Bowel movements are normal—no blood or black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. You had a gastric bypass years ago, and then a G-tube placed, which was removed recently—is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had the G-tube for nutrition, but I asked to have it removed. Since then, the pain and heaving got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your history shows you’ve had ulcers at the surgical site before. We’re concerned that might be flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the dry heaves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, irritation or an ulcer in the stomach remnant can cause nausea and retching, even without vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on IV fluids to keep you hydrated and give you a ‘banana bag’—it has vitamins and electrolytes. You’ve been on pantoprazole and sucralfate at home—we’ll continue those, but through IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’ve been worried about not getting enough nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Right now, we’re supporting you with fluids. We’re planning an upper endoscopy in the next day or two to look at your stomach pouch and the bypass connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under sedation, so you’ll be asleep. It’s very safe. We’ll use it to check for ulcers or inflammation and treat anything we see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m okay with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look stable. White count is a bit low but not concerning. Your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little better today—still some nausea, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’re going to try advancing your diet today—start with a stage 4 bariatric diet. Small portions, soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Things like mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs, pureed soups. Easy to digest. We’ll watch you after the first meal to make sure you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with lunch—no heaving, and you said the food stayed down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I only had a small amount, but it felt okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep you on the IV protonix twice a day for acid suppression. The endoscopy is scheduled for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a chance they’ll find another ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Given your history, we’re especially looking at the anastomosis and the gastric pouch. If we see an ulcer, we can treat it with medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it’s bad, could I need another G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. Most of these can be managed with meds and diet. We’re not planning any tubes unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the endoscopy. You did great. The report shows your bypass anatomy looks good. No issues in the small intestine or connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But… there was something, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small erosion was seen in the top part of your stomach remnant—the cardia. It’s not a full ulcer, but it’s irritated and likely causing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can that heal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll keep you on high-dose pantoprazole twice a day and sucralfate four times a day. Those help protect and heal the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance you to a stage 5 bariatric diet—regular soft foods, but still small portions. No spicy or acidic foods for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Vital signs are stable, you’re tolerating food, and your pain is controlled. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue sucralfate four times a day, pantoprazole twice daily, and metoclopramide as needed for nausea. We’re adjusting your citalopram and aripiprazole doses too—lower now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your surgeon in one week. Call us sooner if you have chest pain, vomiting, black stools, fever, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lifting, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—nothing over 10 pounds until your follow-up. And avoid driving while on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand everything. Thank you for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep resting, stay hydrated, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for worsening dry heaves and abdominal pain following removal of her G-tube, with a history of gastric bypass and anastomotic ulcers. She was hydrated with IV fluids and started on IV proton pump inhibition. By hospital day 2, she tolerated a stage 4 bariatric diet. An upper endoscopy on day 3 revealed a small erosion in the gastric remnant cardia, with otherwise normal findings. She progressed to a stage 5 diet, remained stable, and was discharged home on oral pantoprazole and sucralfate with instructions for follow-up. Her symptoms improved with medical management, and no surgical intervention was required.
